title: Iain McGilchrist: "Great discoveries are not made by following the scientific method"
subtitle: The limits of left-brain thinking
author: Iain McGilchrist
introduction: We assume advances in science are driven by rigorous adherence to the scientific method. Reductive analysis, reason, and evidence are said to be the engines of progress. But according to world-renowned psychiatrist and philosopher Iain McGilchrist, the great advances in science occur not by following a rigid set of rules, but by breaking them. In conversation with Oliver Adelson, he argues that only by seeing the world in its holistic, interconnected form are we able to make the leaps of logic which science needs to discover new paradigms.
body:
Oliver Adelson: The left hemisphere of the brain is said to be the rational, analytic side. And yet it’s your contention that what we’ve had is too much, not too little, of left hemisphere thinking. Can you explain what led you to this view?

Iain McGilchrist: What we’ve got here are two halves of the brain. For evolutionary reasons, all creatures have had to develop two ways of attending to the world, and one is with a very narrow, targeted attention to a detail—they already know what it is, and they know they want to get it, and having it will make them powerful. So that’s very important. One whole half of the brain is dedicated basically to that process. The other half of the brain is doing everything else. It has open, sustained attention to everything, and this is the one that actually understands the whole.

Now, when you come to look at how they construe the world, the left hemisphere sees the world as made up of bits. And the bits are separate from one another. They don’t change, they don’t move, they are fully known, they are explicit. They’re also abstract, they’re taken out of context, they’re categorical in nature, and effectively inanimate—something like a diagram or a map of the world rather than the world itself.

The right hemisphere, however, sees the closest we get to knowing what the world is like. It sees a world in which everything is connected, in which everything is not fixed and unchangeable, but is constantly flowing and changing, in which the implicit is vastly more important than the explicit, in which context is everything. Things are unique and they’re not just exemplars of categories. And this world is a living world, and it presences to us, as Heidegger would have said, rather than just being represented in the way the world of the left is. So that’s it in a very, very brief nutshell.

If the relationship between the world presented by the left hemisphere and reality isn’t simply a mirror relationship, if the left hemisphere doesn’t just mirror reality with its categorical bits—what then is the relationship between the world presented by the right hemisphere and reality? Do you think that is a sort of mirror of the way that reality is, or we need to discard the mirror metaphor altogether?

Well, I don’t think the mirror is terribly helpful, but I suppose I would say that the world as conceived or perceived and understood, most importantly, by the right hemisphere is at least in touch with the experiential world. It is a world where, if you follow its beliefs, you will be, as William James put it about truth, “less likely to be caught out all the time by reality.” And I think that if you understand the world the way the right hemisphere sees it, you will find it’s enormously congruent and explains a lot of the things about the structure of the world that the left hemisphere model—which is, I would say, the absolutely dominant model of our society—would miss.

I don’t agree with Donald Hoffman that we’re just like sitting in a padded cell reading off dials, but that is a fair description of the left hemisphere. The left hemisphere is basically out of touch with reality. The right hemisphere feeds things to it and its job is then to feed that back. It’s rather like putting data into a computer, hoping the computer will spew out the information. The computer doesn’t understand it, but you do, and you put it back into the whole. That is the important thing that you’re trying to understand.

Whereas the right hemisphere is like a room with a window on the world. So when it comes up with an idea, it doesn’t just say, “Oh, this is a marvelous theory.” It says, “Does this actually add up? Is this anything to do with the world as we know it?”

One human enterprise in which left-brain thinking appears to dominate is science. What do you think the implications of your account are for science and for the scientific method?

Well, I’m a great supporter of both science and reason, but I’m also a great believer that they have their limitations. Most good scientists and most philosophers are very well aware of that. Some people who are not terribly aware of these things think that they can answer all our questions. The fact that they can answer very many questions and be extraordinarily helpful servants doesn’t make them the arbiters of everything that we know.

Now, the limitations of science and this method are not as great as one might think. I don’t want to overemphasize it. As I say, there’s a lot to be said for the scientific method. But what people don’t understand is that actually most discoveries in science and in mathematics—the great discoveries—are not made by following the scientific method at all. They were not made by linear paths of logic or algorithms. They were made by suddenly seeing a gestalt—in other words, a whole that is a form irreducible to its parts without loss. That’s a very important idea. And if you think everything can be understood by analysis, you will miss it. Analysis only tells us information that is useful when it’s put back into the context of the whole.

Sometimes I think about a piece of music. You’re attracted to it as a whole; that’s the right hemisphere working. You then try to play it. You break it down in various places, you take it apart analytically, you practice passages over and over, and the piece is a bit of a mess and a bit of a theoretical bodge. And then you go on stage and you have to forget all that and play. And that doesn’t mean that the business of taking it apart and fiddling about with it and practicing bits and fragmenting it wasn’t useful. But at the end it will be a hopeless performance unless that is recohered.

Now, an area in which science is less good is seeing the bigger picture. And I think a lot of the big steps forward have been made by scientists who did see the big picture, famously Einstein. But I could give you forty other examples of scientists and mathematicians, and some of them are in my work, who made their discoveries in a moment of insight, either looking at something, just walking, putting their foot on the step of the bus after going shopping, or, in the case of Einstein, picking up a fiddle and going, “I’ve got it.” And it’s very interesting that these things are not done in the way that science pretends that they should be and are done. So while it’s very good to have a bit of work done in linear thinking, you have to be able to go beyond that.

And all science also has to walk a tightrope between giving up on a paradigm too quickly, too easily, and not shifting early enough. So of course you don’t want science, every time there’s a finding that seems to contradict something that is believed, to go and say, “Well, we’re going to change everything on that basis.” But when the evidence builds up to a certain point, you should adopt a position of, “maybe this is right, maybe we’ve been barking up the wrong tree.” And it’s very rare that public science is humble enough to do that, although some very great scientists have the humility to say that. And I have to say, they’re very often physicists.

I suppose we see the most extreme case of this sort of fractured reality in the dominant paradigms of reductionism and materialism. So do you think that these paradigms are fettering science? Do you think that the dominance of these paradigms perhaps explains why we haven’t seen an Einstein in recent years, for example?

Yes, it’s very interesting, isn’t it, that up until about the 1970s there were a whole lot of Nobel Prizes in science and it made many leaps forward. But more recently it hasn’t. And I think this is to do with stereotypical thinking rather than thinking “outside the box”—more creative thinking, allowing yourself to listen to an intuition to see a form, a shape, a gestalt, as I say, which could lead you to a conclusion. So I think that is stopping science from moving forward.

But another thing is that—and it’s not unconnected, I’m afraid—in a left hemisphere-dominated world, bureaucracy is very top-heavy, and everything has to be legally laid out, and there are rules and procedures and so on. When Thomson discovered the electron, he was just one man. And nowadays a lot of the papers that come out have literally thousands, tens of thousands in some cases, of authors.

This kind of huge enterprise is like a galleon in the face of a skiff that can quickly change direction. And science needs flexibility, and it needs more of the big picture and more imagination. But it doesn’t need to abandon anything that it considers important. It just needs to branch out a bit more.

I want to move on to the mind and consciousness. But before we do that, I just want to touch on the relationship between mind and body, because when people discuss this, it’s often assumed that the body is straightforward and it’s the mind which we have to crack. But one point which some philosophers like Noam Chomsky have made is that we don’t understand matter anymore than we understand mind. The notion itself of matter as traditionally conceived is very problematic. Could you say a bit about that?

We have very little time, sadly, but it’s a totally fascinating topic. What I would say is that he’s entirely right. Many physicists have themselves said that if we reduce everything to matter, then we’re faced with the question, “But what the hell is matter?” And physicists will readily say they don’t know.

So we haven’t gone from somewhere mysterious to somewhere clearer. But what we have done is create a barrier between two things that I don’t think should be kept entirely separate. To be very brief about this, I am a panpsychist. It’s an odd-sounding position, but my position is that consciousness was never derived from matter. There was never a moment in which suddenly consciousness emerged like a magic trick out of matter.

The more rational position is that consciousness is, if you like, a building block of the universe. The way I would put it is that it’s an ontological primitive. It’s something that isn’t accounted for in any other terms. It is what it is. And I believe that everything that exists in the cosmos exists within that field, that very large field of consciousness, and partakes of it. One of the things that I go on to suppose—and again, sadly, I have no time to give any rationale for this at all, but I have written at length about it—is that not only are matter and consciousness not entirely separate from one another, but that actually what we call matter is a way in which consciousness may manifest itself. It manifests itself in many ways, and one of them is as matter.

Why? Because matter offers two things that consciousness on its own doesn’t. One is resistance, and the other is persistence. And without resistance, anything goes. It’s much too vague. But without persistence, everything goes. So you need both resistance and persistence for every act of creation. And matter is what achieves that.

People may say, “Well, matter doesn’t look like consciousness. It doesn’t seem to have the same qualities at all. How can that be?” But I would say, “Look, water has phases. In one, it’s transparent, it’s translucent. It runs across your hand. It’s the thing we know that flows. And then there is this other thing, which is a huge block of something very cold and hard. And it can’t be moved except with great effort. It’s hard enough to split your head open. But that is water as well. It’s just what we call ice. And in this room, there are tons of water suspended in the air without which I couldn’t speak to you. And none of these looks remotely like the other or has the same qualities.”

There are some other accounts, of course, that people have about how we might crack the mind. And usually these make use of different metaphors. Of course, in the case of Freud, he had his hydraulics. Now we’ve updated to computers and machines. Is this just the latest metaphor? Or is there something fundamentally different about it in comparison to the past metaphors that people have used to understand the mind?

Well, I think that the machine metaphor has been creeping up on us since the end of the 17th and certainly since the early 18th century, and it has become the default metaphor with which science accounts for things.

Scientists sometimes talk as if metaphors should be avoided, but what they don’t understand is that anything that is complex and sui generis can only be understood by a metaphor. And they are therefore inevitable. The question is, have you got the right one? And if they think they haven’t got a metaphor, they’ve got a metaphor of the machine nonetheless. And that has its own insidious quality, partly because it isn’t recognized as such. So I do think it’s very important that we change the metaphor. And I think metaphors such as music and water—I mean, they may sound terribly airy-fairy, but believe me, they are very important ways of understanding the connectivity of things and the ways in which they interrelate and change.

I’m not suggesting that they are the truth about anything in some very simplistic way, because I think the whole problem is that some scientists believe that they have simple truths. But there are no simple truths. All truths are contextual. All truths are modified by the way in which they’re understood and by whom they’re understood and how they are discussed. And so it behoves us to be very careful about how we pay attention to the world, because the way in which we attend to it changes what it is altogether that we see there. If we attend to a body in a certain way, we see just a machine. If we attend to a body in another way, like Blake, we see something miraculous that is holy. And I believe that is just as legitimate a way to understand the body if you’ve lived a life. And of course an AI machine has not—it has no body. It cannot suffer, it cannot love, it doesn’t know that it’s going to die—none of the things that humans deal with. And so it’s a very, very poor guide to how we should think.

On the issue of AI: AI has been remarkably successful in some of the left-brain tasks. You see that with large language models. Could there be an AI model of what the right hemisphere is doing? Or is that never going to happen?

I don’t think that can ever happen. Because what it requires is, in a way, an ability to see that things are not best structured according to principles.

It’s rather like Zen. If you admire a Zen thinker, you then say, “So how do I become Zen?” And the Zen master will say to you something completely absurd. And that’s a way of bringing you up against the fact that the idea that there are steps or procedures or principles will not work. It’s something beyond that. You have to, in a way, make a leap. And the right hemisphere is the world that deals with these leaps of insight. It really does. In particular, the right superior temporal gyrus and sulcus are very important for this. So it’s in that world that we see the unexpected, the new.

The left hemisphere sees only repeats of what it already knows and it’s very happy with that. So as long as it stays within the confines of a self-referring system, that’s fine. And an AI can be a self-referring system. And, unfortunately, the problems that come from self-referring systems are beginning to make themselves evident. For example, making stuff up and thinking that you’re always right, which are both features of people with right hemisphere damage relying on the left hemisphere. They make things up. It’s called confabulation. They are prone to delusion. Most of the important delusions are dependent on right hemisphere failure, not on left. And they begin to be absolutely clear that they are right. And the more we move into this modern world, the more I see people with very stupid ideas who think they’re absolutely right and that anyone who disagrees with them is completely wrong and must be completely cancelled.

One striking part of your account is that there seems to be this oscillation in different epochs. For example, you argue that in the Renaissance there was a predominance of right hemisphere thinking, which swung to left hemisphere thinking in the Enlightenment, and then with Romanticism it swung back to the right. I think most people would argue that we are in a left hemisphere-dominant society. Do you think that the next epoch we see in these grand terms will be dominated by the right hemisphere?

Well, of course I’m very much hopeful of that. And the way I see it is that there tends to be an overarching trend over these pendulum swings, which is toward the left. So there may be slight corrections, like romanticism, but then it goes on further towards the left. So I’m not really sure. But I live in hope. And reasons for hope are that people who think they can predict the future are very often wrong and end up with egg on their face.

People are resourceful. As long as we don’t believe ourselves to be machines in the way AI and the culture of AI makes us think, as long as we realize that we are unpredictably creative and responsive creatures, I think that there will be a redress. And I think this is already beginning among the young. And the young are the future. My soul goes out to the young who are saying, “Enough of this reductive materialism,” which is such a trivial philosophy. It can be taken apart so quickly and easily, and it misses out everything of importance.

So be loyal to the things you know that call to you, which will be things that call to you spiritually and through things like beauty and sheer truth and goodness. Those are the things not to allow to be degraded into ticking boxes and procedures that can be assessed by a machine. They can’t.

On that note, Iain McGilchrist, thank you very much for joining me.

Thank you.
